content: The varicella (chickenpox) vaccine is an important immunization designed to protect against chickenpox, a common childhood illness. While chickenpox is typically mild, it can lead to serious complications, particularly in young infants and adults. The disease is characterized by a rash, itching, fever, and fatigue, and in severe cases, it can result in skin infections, scarring, pneumonia, brain damage, or even death. The virus spreads through airborne transmission or direct contact with fluid from chickenpox blisters. Additionally, individuals who have had chickenpox are at risk of developing shingles, a painful rash, later in life. Before the vaccine was introduced, approximately 11,000 people were hospitalized, and about 100 people died annually in the United States due to chickenpox. The chickenpox vaccine is highly effective in preventing the disease. Most vaccinated individuals do not contract chickenpox, and if they do, the symptoms are usually mild, with fewer blisters, a lower likelihood of fever, and faster recovery. Who Should Receive the Chickenpox Vaccine and When Routine Vaccination for Children: Children who have never had chickenpox should receive two doses of the vaccine. The first dose is recommended between 12–15 months of age, and the second dose between 4–6 years of age. The second dose can be administered earlier if at least three months have passed since the first dose. Vaccination for Adolescents and Adults: Individuals aged 13 years or older who have never had chickenpox or the vaccine should receive two doses, spaced at least 28 days apart. Catch-Up Vaccination: Children or adolescents who are not fully vaccinated should receive one or two doses, depending on their age. Consult a healthcare provider for specific guidance. The chickenpox vaccine can be administered alongside other vaccines, including the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine, as part of a combination vaccine called MMRV. Who Should Not Receive the Chickenpox Vaccine or Should Delay Vaccination Individuals who have experienced a life-threatening allergic reaction to gelatin, the antibiotic neomycin, or a previous dose of the chickenpox vaccine should not receive it. Those who are moderately or severely ill at the time of vaccination should wait until they recover. Pregnant women should delay vaccination until after childbirth and avoid becoming pregnant for one month following vaccination. Certain individuals should consult their doctor before vaccination, including those with: HIV/AIDS or other conditions affecting the immune system. Ongoing treatment with immune-suppressing drugs, such as steroids, for two weeks or longer. Any type of cancer or those undergoing cancer treatment with radiation or chemotherapy. A recent blood transfusion or administration of other blood products. Side Effects of the Chickenpox Vaccine The chickenpox vaccine is significantly safer than contracting the disease itself. Most individuals experience no issues after vaccination. However, as with any medical intervention, there is a small risk of serious side effects, such as severe allergic reactions. The likelihood of the vaccine causing serious harm or death is extremely low. Mild Side Effects Soreness or swelling at the injection site (occurs in about 1 in 5 children and up to 1 in 3 adolescents and adults). Fever (affects fewer than 1 in 10 individuals). Mild rash, which may appear up to a month after vaccination (affects fewer than 1 in 20 individuals). In rare cases, these individuals may transmit the virus to household members. Note: The MMRV vaccine has been associated with higher rates of fever (up to 1 in 5 individuals) and measles-like rash (about 1 in 20 individuals) compared to separate administration of the MMR and varicella vaccines. Moderate Side Effects Seizures caused by fever (affects fewer than 1 in 1,000 individuals). Severe Side Effects Pneumonia (very rare). Other serious problems, such as severe brain reactions and low blood counts, have been reported but are so rare that experts cannot definitively link them to the vaccine. What to Do in Case of a Moderate or Severe Reaction Be vigilant for any unusual symptoms, such as high fever or behavioral changes. Signs of a severe allergic reaction may include difficulty breathing, hoarseness or wheezing, hives, paleness, weakness, rapid heartbeat, or dizziness. If any of these occur: Contact a doctor or seek medical attention immediately. Provide details about the reaction, including the date, time, and when the vaccine was administered. Ask your healthcare provider to file a Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) form, or you can report it yourself by calling 1-800-822-7967 or visiting the VAERS website. National Vaccine Injury Compensation Program In the rare event of a serious reaction to a vaccine, a federal program exists to help cover the costs of care for those affected. For more information, call 1-800-338-2382 or visit the program’s website. How to Learn More Consult your doctor or healthcare provider for additional information. They can provide the vaccine package insert or recommend other resources. Contact your local or state health department’s immunization program. Reach out to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) by calling 1-800-232-4636 (1-800-CDC-INFO) or visiting the National Immunization Program’s website.
